one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban praises the Supreme Court for resolving two crucial electoral roadblocks 'with commendable alacrity and speed' -- both threatening to upset preparations for the 2016 presidential elections. On Dec 8, the Court junked the Kabataan Party-list petition challenging two Comelec resolutions that fixed the voter registration deadline on Oct 31, 2015; on Dec 16, it trashed Kabataan's second petition questioning the 'No Bio-No Boto' policy and lifted its earlier TRO. Whether or not we agree with the decisions, our people should applaud the speed and encourage similar dispatch on all election-related matters. On the first case, petitioners argued the Oct 31 cutoff is more than two months earlier than what the Voters Registration Law (RA 8189) provides, effectively disenfranchising 2.4 million voters who failed to register. After ordering the Comelec to comment on Dec 7, the Court 'Voila' issued its unanimous three-page resolution the very next day dismissing the petition. It held that RA 8189 'merely provides that registration shall no longer be allowed during the period of 120 days before a regular election or, in this case, beyond Jan 8, 2016. It does not, however, mandate the period for registration should be up to such time.' On the second case, 'No Bio-No Boto' is a short, catchy Filipino restatement of the Mandatory Biometrics Registration Law of 2013 (RA 10367) which deactivates voters who fail to have their biometrics validated by the last day for registration. The 18-month Comelec public information campaign (May 2014 - Oct 31, 2015) ran concurrent with continuing voter registrations and gave sufficient notice. Justice Estela Perlas-Bernabe -- and CJ agrees -- explained that a distinction should be made between voters' 'qualifications' and their 'registration': registration is merely a preparatory step toward voting and 'is not one of the elements that make the citizen a qualified voter,' while the biometrics requirement rids the voters' list of 'ghost' and 'flying' voters. CJ acknowledges he initially sympathized with petitioners' disenfranchisement concern but had to consider that extension would imperil the Comelec's meticulously planned preparations and might result in electoral chaos. He enumerates the Comelec's Project of Precincts (POP) logistics: 54.5 million registered voters across 373,786 established precincts and 94,000 clustered precincts in 42,029 barangays, 1,490 municipalities, 144 cities, and 81 provinces; POP data drives boards of election inspectors, forms/supplies allocation, vote-counting machines deployment, and budgets; ballot templates for 18,083 elective positions with at least 45,800 candidates; 1,953 ballot faces to be posted at the Comelec website for candidate counter-checking before final printing. Rather than risk a chaotic poll and to ensure a credible and orderly election on May 9, 2016, he concludes it is much better to abide by and uphold the Comelec's timetable.
